articles.text: Piedmont Scout Troop 15 held a Court of Honor on May 14 at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse. The highlight was the presentation of the Eagle Award, Scouting’s highest honor, to longtime Troop 15 Scout Nate Woodley. Families mingled in the Courtyard before the ceremony, enjoying a pot-luck supper. articles.text: As part of their participation in the East Bay’s 30th annual Bike Day, the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division set up an energizer station at the corner of Highland and Vista Avenue for cyclists. It drew more than 30 visitors, the event’s highest turnout since the city began participating in Bike Day. “It was a fun and lively morning, and we were thrilled to see so many different types of cyclists – people commuting to work, to school, riding with children, riding for exercise. It was a fun and inspiring morning,” said Echa Schneider, the city’s Communications Manager. On Thursday, May 16, from 7 a.m. to 9 a.m., riders could stop by the energizer station to grab coffee and snacks provided by Mulberry’s Market as well as free reusable tote bags and reusable straw kits. Additionally, cyclists visiting the station were entered into a raffle to win a bike cleaning essentials kit from the Sustainability Division. The Energizer Station was hosted by the City’s sustainability staff with support from other departments. PPD Officer Tyler Petit was present to help participants sign up for the PPD’s free Safe Bike Program. Bike Day was founded in the East Bay in 1994 to celebrate bicycles as a fun and healthy way to get to work, as well as to give those who don’t normally use their bikes to commute an opportunity to try it out. With transportation accounting for almost half of Piedmont’s total greenhouse gas emissions, encouraging more residents to use greener commute options is vital to meeting the city’s climate action targets. articles.text: On January 15, Piedmont Key Club, a student-led club at PHS and a part of the larger Kiwanis nonprofit organization, started off the new year with a soccer equipment drive in collaboration with Soccer Without Borders. Soccer Without Borders is a nonprofit organization based in Oakland that fosters positive change in communities by giving refugee and immigrant youth a place to feel comfortable being themselves, allowing them to create connections in their community, and teaching them valuable life skills through their love for soccer. But to be able to make this opportunity available and affordable to underserved youth, the organization needs donations. Seeing an opportunity to support the organization by collecting used soccer equipment from students at Piedmont schools, Piedmont Key Club decided to host a soccer equipment drive with collection bins placed on school campuses. Students in the club spread the word about the drive by making posters. The drive was a major success, and resulted in collecting 37 pairs of cleats, 13 soccer balls, five bins of soccer clothes, one bin of shin guards, and one bin of soccer socks, as well as gear like pop-up goals, pennies, and soccer bags. Piedmont Key Club was able to make this drive possible because of the planning and coordination of the club’s leadership and the hard work of the students in the club to get the word out. The club, whose goal is to help PHS students give back to their community, gives students opportunities to perform small acts of community service during their Wednesday lunch meetings in room 302 of the PHS STEAM building. It also provides students with information about other volunteer opportunities outside of school and hosts its own events such as bake sales.

articles.text: The Greater Good Science Center at the University of California in Berkeley is a leader in the field of applied positive psychology. I was able to sit down with Jason Marsh, Executive Director of the GGSC, to discuss their work, positive psychology, and how Piedmonters can get involved. Through an online magazine, podcasts, videos, quizzes, and workshops, the GGSC reaches over a million people each month. Their website is particularly geared toward educators, ensuring that the latest insights into human happiness and social harmony are shared with those shaping future generations. The GGSC’s mission revolves around understanding and fostering positive emotions and social cohesion. This mission is underscored by the belief that personal wellbeing significantly contributes to the broader health of communities. As the center’s work shows, fostering compassion, curiosity, and kindness within individuals can weave these values into the fabric of society, promoting social peace and harmony. The journey of integrating GGSC’s principles into daily life begins with understanding the true nature of happiness. According to Marsh, “happiness encompasses two dimensions: momentary positive emotions like joy and hope, and a deeper sense of life satisfaction and purpose.” Marsh emphasizes that understanding the roots of sociological problems and addressing them paves the way for utilizing positive psychology effectively. This holistic approach acknowledges the necessity of meeting basic needs before personal development can flourish. Positive psychology’s focus on resilience and meaning offers tools for everyone, including those grappling with depression and negative thoughts, to achieve a more balanced and fulfilling life. Piedmont residents, many of whom have strong ties to UC Berkeley, are in a unique position to engage with GGSC’s resources. The center was founded by Berkeley alumni Tom and Ruth, who aimed to honor their daughter’s memory and give back to the university. The center’s initiatives are deeply integrated with UC Berkeley, involving university-funded staff, graduate fellows, and research assistants. Piedmonters can subscribe to the free newsletter, which provides regular updates on content and events, or listen to the “Science of Happiness” podcast. GGSC also offers various events, including free webinars and paid workshops, which are excellent opportunities for deeper engagement. Volunteering at these events is another way to contribute, especially as in-person activities ramp up post-COVID. For those interested in further exploring the field of wellbeing, Marsh recommends “Self-Compassion” by Kristen Neff and “The Myths of Happiness” by Sonja Lyubomirsky. These books provide valuable insights into personal growth and the science of happiness. Getting involved with the GGSC offers Piedmont residents a chance to enhance their own lives while contributing to a more compassionate society. positive psychology, you can help foster a culture of wellbeing that extends far beyond personal happiness to create a more interconnected community in Piedmont. articles.text: The Alan Harvey Theater hosted Piedmont High School’s Spring Concert on Tuesday, May 21, directed by 1st year band teacher Trevor Meseroll, with music by the Symphonic Band and Jazz Bands. The evening started off with the Symphonic Band performing Barry Manilow’s “Copacabana.” The ensemble then moved into pieces titled “Let’s Groove” by Wayne Vaugh and Maurice White and “Pirates of the Caribbean” by Hans Zimmer. PHS Senior Edwin Tang provided senior leadership for the ensemble on flute. He received accolades last week at the Senior Awards Night as “Outstanding Senior in Symphonic Band.” Photos by Sophie Hess Singer Claire Weiss The PHS Jazz Band presented four different combos of musicians during the show; music for the Jazz Band Combos were preLaurel Minor (left) on trombone, Kalyani Spieckerman on tenor sax, and Milo Bakshi on alto sax Edwin Tang (left), Henry Nielsen, Peter Stokes, Alden Meil, Ryan St. John, Will Kennedy, and Miles Antaya pared by Band Clinicians Claire Chaix and Natalie John. Senior Will Kennedy on Alto Sax, was announced as the winner of “Outstanding Senior in Jazz Band” as well. PHS junior Claire Weiss, a talented vocalist and trumpeter, handled vocals for The Jazz Combo II. She sang “I Know You Know” by Esperanza Spalding and “Lilac Wine” by James Shelton. The Jazz band played a number of songs including “Higher Ground” by Stevie Wonder and “Agua De Beber” by Antonio Carlos Jobim. The evening concluded with the recognition of Piedmont seniors who will soon be graduating. Senior Ryan St. John on drums Miles Antaya (left) and Will Kennedy on sax Dorothy Nemeth on cello Symphonic Band: (front row) Matt Steimle (left), Caitilin Boothby, and Shayna Chau. articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School baseball team has etched its name in the annals of East Bay Middle School League history as the regular season and tournament champions. Their remarkable journey culminated in an undefeated season with a decisive 5-0 victory on Tuesday, May 21, over the reigning champions, the Cobras from Berkeley’s M.L. King Middle School,. Piedmont Middle School made its debut in the EBMSL this year, fielding its first-ever middle school baseball team. Comprising twelve 7th graders and 13 eighth graders, the team quickly established itself. Pitching and defense were the cornerstones of the Scots’ championship campaign. In the title game, Jimmy Lagios took the mound and gave up only two hits in six shutout innings. Henry Stein broke the scoreless deadlock in the third inning with an RBI groundout, driving in Dylan Toyama from third base. The fourth inning saw Aiden Bell and Orion Sachs deliver crucial singles, with Bell scoring on a fielder’s choice off Max Fujimoto’s bat. Fujimoto’s steal of home added another run to Piedmont’s tally. In the fifth inning, Mateo Long, Stein, and Toyama each contributed singles, scoring two more runs. Massimo Mittone, who had played flawlessly at shortstop, stepped in to relieve Lagios on the mound in the seventh inning. He threw just 10 pitches to close out the game. Jonah Cha-Foster, a stalwart behind the plate, transitioned to shortstop to replace Mittone after six innings of stellar play at catcher. Lagios boasted an impressive 0.276 ERA over 25 innings throughout the season, while Mittone’s ERA was an astounding 0.00 in 11 innings. Jonah Cha-Foster and Aaron Bennett also made significant contributions on the mound. Cha-Foster’s expertise behind the plate complemented Lagios’s pitching, while Sachs handled the bulk of the team’s innings behind the plate, while excelling also as a pitcher and second baseman. Sachs and Cha-Foster led the team in hitting, closely followed by Long, Toyama, and Sorenson. Max Fujimoto’s play in center field was a defensive highlight all season. Head coach Josh Campuzano, a former player in the league with Montera Hr. High in Montclair, summed up the team’s success: “We knew we had a talented group of middle schoolers, but playing in this highly competitive league against top-tier opponents was no small feat. The dominant pitching rotation of Lagios, Mittone, Bennett, Cha-Foster, and Sachs proved insurmountable.” The future looks promising for the Scots. The twelve 7th graders took on varsity squads from six schools and emerged unbeaten. With such talent and continued hard work, Piedmont Middle School baseball is poised for continued success. articles.text: Piedmont High School sailors who are part of the sailing team at Encinal Yacht Club in Alameda wrapped up a successful year with a celebration and awards dinner on Sunday evening, May 19. A total of 17 high school teams participated. Junior Sophie Hess presented awards to seniors Mica Jorcino and Peter Stokes, thanking them both for making it such a fun season filled with lots of improvement. Now in its 18th year, Encinal’s High School Sailing program has had 66 sailors move on to college level sailing at schools around the country with 22 serving as captains of their teams. Of those 66, 18 are currently active including PHS alumni Conor Kim who sails for UC Santa Cruz and Sara Govert who coaches for EYC. Peter Stokes will be sailing for UC Berkeley and Mica Jorcino for Cal Poly in San Luis Obispo in the fall. The Encinal Yacht Club (EYC) High School Sailing Program is for students in grades 8-12 with or without sailing experience. Participants attend weekly practices at EYC and weekend regattas in the Bay Area and Southern California from fall through spring. Regattas are organized by Pacific Coast Interscholastic Sailing Association. The EYC Junior Sailing Program works in partnership with high schools throughout the East Bay who have teams or clubs that participate in the Interscholastic Sailing Association (ISSA). Rising 8th -12th graders are welcome to join Piedmont’s sailing team. There are summer opportunities at EYC for kids of all ages and levels. For more information, contact Sophie Hess (shess@piedmont.k12.ca.us) or visit https://www.encinal.org/ youth-programs/high-school. articles.text: Show at de Young will draw florists and designers from across the Bay Area Next week, local florist J. Miller Flowers will participate in the de Young Museum’s annual Bouquets to Art event for its 25th consecutive year. Bouquets to Art, which itself is celebrating its 40th anniversary this year, is an event that allows museumgoers to engage with the de Young’s expansive collections in a novel way – through floral interpretations of some of its most classic works. Each year, the leading floral designers of the Bay Area draw inspiration from a particular work in the museum and create a floral arrangement inspired by the work, which is then displayed in front of the original art piece at the de Young for museumgoers to see. From sculptures to sketches, nothing remains off-limits as a source of inspiration. J. Miller Flowers reinterprets The Niagara River at the Cataract (left) and Horseshoe Falls from below the High Bank (c. 1832) by Gustav Grunewald for Bouquets to Art 2012. Designed by Valerie Lee, Maureen Owens and Robbin Lee. Photo by Valerie Lee J. Miller Flowers reinterprets Singing Beach, Manchester, MA (1863) by Martin Johnson Heade for Bouquets to Art 2022. Designed by Valerie Lee, Robbin Lee, Jacqueline McGillicuddy and Robby Ow. Staff photo Robbin Lee (left) and Valerie Lee, co-owners of J. Miller Flowers, will participate in the de Young’s Bouquets to Art event for their 25th year. The event lasts for six days, Tuesday to Sunday, June 4-9. “It’s one of my favorite weeks of the year because it brings together friends, art, and flowers while raising much-needed funds for the Fine Arts Museum in San Francisco, specifically the de Young Museum and the Legion of Honor,” said Valerie Lee, co-owner of J. Miller Flowers on Piedmont Avenue. “And to be surrounded with flower-filled art galleries in June is just glorious to me.” In previous years, co-owners Valerie Lee and Robbin Lee have interpreted paintings of dresses, sunsets and swans as striking, vibrant flower arrangements. This year, the duo will be interpreting the de Young’s collection of New Guinean ceremonial shields. “I’m more intrigued with paintings or sculpture. However, this year I knew I wanted to perhaps do something with tropical flowers. So, the New Guinea wooden shields lent themselves well to that idea.” To suit her vision, Valerie Lee ordered her exhibit’s tropical flowers directly from Hilo, Hawaii, one of the largest tropical flower growers on the island. Her entry will be displayed in front of the de Young’s Shields of New Guinea in Gallery 20 on the second floor adjacent to the main staircase. Lee said that the most difficult part of the exhibition has always been keeping the flowers fresh between showings. “That’s the challenge of participating in this. You want to make sure every museumgoer has a chance to see the same, refreshing flowers.” The event will also feature a raffle of fresh arrangements from the museum’s flower cart, and eventgoers are encouraged to take part in engaging lectures with renowned designers and authors happening throughout the week. Opening night begins at 5:30 p.m. on Monday, June 4. Complimentary parking in the Music Concourse Parking Garage is provided for all Opening Night attendees. Food and drinks will be prepared by McCalls Catering & Events. The de Young Museum is located at 50 Hagawara Tea Garden Dr in San Francisco. Tickets can be purchased online at www. famsf.org or by phone at (888) 901-6645. Advance tickets are required for this event.

articles.text: Community members flocked to J. Miller Flowers last weekend for something more than a bouquet of flowers. It was the opening of a nature-themed pop art exhibit featuring the art of former Piedmont Middle School art teacher Kim Lipkin, a Piedmont resident, as well as others. The exhibition was held in a behind-the-scenes side room at J. Miller Flowers that is typically used for cutting and cleaning flowers, where visitors could enjoy glasses of lemonade and fresh rosemary shortbread while browsing and purchasing paintings from the gallery. The show was open Friday, May 24, to Sunday, May 26. Organizers estimate that it had nearly 100 attendees per day. “It’s all about building community. That’s what any business is about,” said Valerie Lee, co-owner of J. Miller Flowers with her sister Robbin Lee. The show featured more than 125 pieces of artwork for sale by artists Kim Lipkin, Heather Piazza, Claire Finne, Hannah Avner, Robert Ow, Lorinne Lee, Jacqueline McGillicuddy, Andrew Ameral and Valerie Lee herself. Although the art at the show had a variety of subjects, Lipkin focused nearly her entire selection on paintings of bright, multicolored floral arrangements. “Flowers are very different from one another, and there are many different varieties to see. I think that’s how life is in a lot of ways,” said Lipkin. “Even the people who I surround myself with on a daily basis are all so different and yet still similar. I feel like that experience is simply part of being alive.” Lipkin describes her style as a mix of impressionism and surrealism accented with bright, swirling colors. Lipkin said that she became involved in the exhibit entirely by chance. “I’ve known Valerie off and on for years, but my husband and all of his friends went to school with her,” she explained. A few weeks ago while she was in the flower shop, when Lee invited Lipkin to participate. “I’d heard of it before but never gotten to participate. So now, I’m just thrilled I get to do it this time.” Lipkin taught art at Piedmont Middle School for 20 years before retiring in 2016. She has lived in Piedmont for 38 years. J. articles.text: Marking its historic 50th anniversary, Kronos Quartet will perform four concerts on consecutive days at SF Jazz’s Miner Auditorium in June. Founded in Seattle in 1973, Kronos Quartet has received more than 40 awards, including three Grammy Awards and the Polar Music, Avery Fisher, and Edison Klassiek Oeuvre Prizes. More than 1000 works have been written for the group, which has been praised for the inclusiveness of its repertoire. Kronos Quartet is the most well-known and nationally recognized string quartet based in San Francisco. The Quartet members are violinists David Harrington and John Sherba, violist Hank Dutt, and cellist Paul Wiancko, who performed at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in a Piedmont Kronos Quartet includes David Harrington and John Sherba (violin), Hank Dutt (viola), and Paul Wiancko (cello) Chamber Music Festival concert. This year’s Kronos Festival comes home to San Francisco in a four-day festival June 20-23. It will showcase Kronos musicians and a host of special guests, featuring world premieres and the final Kronos performances by violinist John Sherba and violist Hank Dutt. Miner Auditorium is located at 201 Franklin Street in San Francisco. For tickets and details of each concert, visit https:// kronosquartet.org/kronos-festival-2024/

The play catapulted Williams to fame and tells the story of the dreamer Tom Wingfield, his mother Amanda, and his sister, Laura. With their father absent and the Great Depression underway, the siblings find comfort in alcohol, movies and writing. When a gentleman caller arrives for dinner, the Wingfield family’s lives are suddenly turned upside down. The cast includes San Francisco Playhouse founder Susi Damilano, Nicole Javier, William Thomas Hodgson, Jake Fong, Aleisha Lew and Kenna Tanaka. The show is on stage six days a week. articles.text: Tickets for the symphonic and orchestral Festival Napa Valley are on sale now. The summer festival pairs innovative classical, jazz, contemporary, opera, and dance productions with Napa Valley’s unparalleled food and wine scene. “We present dazzling talent on spectacular stages surrounded by the incomparable beauty of Napa Valley,” said Festival President and CEO Richard Walker. “It’s a one-of-a-kind experience and a highlight of the year for guests and artists, both returning and new.” Performances take place on the Festival Napa Valley Stage at Charles Krug Winery in St. Helena, the Ecolab Theatre and Jackson Family Wines Amphitheater at Copia in Napa, Nickel & Nickel in Oakville, and at wineries, resorts, and estates throughout Napa Valley. Now in its 18th season, the festival opens on July 6 with a concert by musicians from The Frost School at Festival Napa Valley’s Blackburn Music Academy. The Academy is an immersive summer conservatory for emerging professional instrumentalists in the idyllic setting of Napa Valley, and is led by a distinguished core faculty of musicians from The Frost School of Music at the University of Miami and leading orchestras and institutions. “We welcome locals and visitors to enjoy the best days of summer,” said Robin Baggett, Chairman of the nonprofit Festival’s Board of Directors. “We are thrilled to provide exceptional programming and food and wine events that showcase the very best of Napa Valley.” For full programming and to purchase tickets. visit https://festivalnapavalley.org/calendar/festival-live-frost-recital-0706/. articles.text: Cellist Sheku Kanneh-Mason will perform with the San Francisco Symphony in three performances led by Esa-Pekka Salonen June 13 through 15. Kanneh-Mason is a British cellist who, at age 17, won the 2016 BBC Young Musician award and was the first Black musician to win the competition since its creation in 1978. He played at the wedding of Prince Harry to Meghan Markle in 2018 under the direction of Christopher Warren-Green. articles.text: Saturday, June 1, 6:30 p.m. Claudia Marseille Book Launch At age four, Claudia Marseille was diagnosed with a severe hearing loss. With determination and the help of powerful hearing aids, she learned to hear, speak and lipread. After earning master’s degrees in archaeology and in public policy, and finally an MFA, she developed a career in photography and painting. She ran a fine art portrait photography studio for 15 years before becoming a full-time painter, and has played classical piano much of her life. articles.text: Diversity is one of the spices of life. That’s the way it was on Friday and Saturday in the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Friday’s spice was an out-of-the-ordinary string quartet concert and on Saturday a spicy chorus. Let’s start with the Circadian String Quartet concert on Friday. The repertoire was mostly modern – at least it had a very modern feel. While Debussy is not considered an avant-garde composer, the arrangements by second violinist David Ryther gave Debussy a modern feel. The quartet itself is very well-balanced tonally, and they present a very mature musical perspective to everything they play. Another thing they do very well is blend politics with music. This will be even more powerful if you buy into their political philosophy. I try to keep an open mind. Circadian’s outlook on the music is both thoughtful and disturbing. The results are never less than interesting. The second half of the concert featured the world premiere of David Ryther’s opera Euridice’s Defiance. The composer has a great gift for melody. This was obvious in all of his works for string quartet. His opera featured guest alto soloist Leslie Bonnet, a last-minute substitute. The results were excellent. There was one section which fell apart, but I think that if they had continued, no one would have known. The work was inspiring. After the concert, a splendid feast rewarded the audience and the performers. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, May 29, 2024 The Musical Gourmet Saturday at the PCA The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The concert the following evening, titled “Notes and letters: an evening of Brahms and the Schumanns,” was also out of the ordinary. It was a concert by Clerestory, a chorus I had never heard of prior to Saturday. Their concert formed a seamless program, completely unified musically and emotionally. The group is balanced musically and their diction is the best I have ever heard from a chorus. The language of the evening was entirely German. There was only one place where I heard a semblance of an American accent. Otherwise everything was absolutely idiomatic – and that is impressive. Another thing they do impressively is to change the formation of the chorus. They move with the precision of a championship marching band. I asked one of the singers why they do that and he explained that they all share the conducting responsibilities. While variety is one of the spices of life, the teamwork exemplified by the Circadian String Quartet and the Clerestory vocal ensemble was a beauty to behold. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré It’s possible that Gran Torino will be Clint Eastwood’s last film as an actor, so it seems appropriate that his role in this film seems a solid reprise of his earlier, now iconic characters. Over the last 30 years Eastwood has cut a wide swath through Hollywood and our popular culture. Beginning with spaghetti westerns made in Italy, such as A Fistful of Dollars and The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, he went on to create the character Dirty Harry, the rogue, jaw-clenching cop who grimaces, squints and asks the bank robber, “You feel lucky? Well, punk, doya?” And of course there were those five words that made their way into our language: “Go ahead, make my day.” In fact, watching Eastwood in Gran Torino portraying Walt Kowalski, a retired auto worker who has just lost his wife, his face deeply lined, his grizzled hair thinning, the rude, gruff mannerisms so familiar, it is clear that Eastwood has always played a variation of himself. Kowalski is Dirty Harry. But he’s also the Carmel DJ in Play Misty for Me, and Rowdy Yates in the television series Wagon Train, the righteous western homesteader in Unforgiven, or the G.I. hunting a German gold cache in Kelly’s Heroes. Fearless as an actor, Eastwood has never been averse to stepping away from the hard-shelled persona he perfected with Harry, He starred in the musical Paint Your Wagon, Anyway But Loose with an orangutan) as a supporting actor, and the romance, The Bridges of Madison County. What has surprised his audience the most, perhaps, s the fine work Eastwood has produced as a director, making such remarkable films as Mystic River, Million Dollar Baby, The Changeling, and the two-film saga about Iwo Jima from the American and Japanese points of view. In Gran Torino, Eastwood inhabits the character of Kowalski and then some. The man is bigoted, narrow of mind, without patience or tolerance; yet, he is also decent, principled and courageous. articles.text: Released in 1993, Free Willy is a family friendly drama that will undoubtedly appeal to a new generation of kids. At the center of this most engaging film are a 7,000 pound Orca whale, named Willy, and a 12-year-old boy, Jessie (Jason James Richter), who are both struggling to adjust to their situations. For Willy, captured while swimming with his pod (think family), it’s the confines of the Northwest Adventure theme park. Jesse, an orphan who was abandoned by his mother at a very early age, grew up in various foster homes, but prefers to hustles on the streets with his urchin buds, scrounging for spare change, and begging for food from the back door of local restaurants. Both Willy and Jesse have an attitude. Willy refuses to work with his trainer, Rae (Lori Petty), and Jesse is surly and filled with resentment at life in general. It’s obvious that if something doesn’t happen to turn Jesse around, he will slip through the cracks and be lost for good. One night, Jesse sneaks into a theme park with a can of spray paint, intent on leaving behind his signature graffiti. He begins with a window overlooking one of the large water tanks where the Orcas perform. He is interrupted by the police who give him three mandatory options: return the next day and clean the window, move in with a foster family, Glen and Annie Greenwood (Jane AtkinJason James Richter and Keiko in Free Willy son and Michel Madsen), who have agreed to give him a home, or take a hard pass and go to juvi. Not eager to go to jail, Jesse agrees to live with the Greenwoods, and returns to the park to scrub the observation window. Walking down by the tank, Jesse is warned by Rae to be careful, there’s an Orca just below the surface. Ignoring Rae, of course, he slips and falls in. But to the surprise of Rae and other park employees, to include the owners of Northwest, Willy gently lifts Jesse out of the water and places him gently onto the side of the pool. Now living with the Greenwoods, Jesse sneaks out at night, and returns to the tank and sits on the side, playing his harmonica. Willy hears him and swims over. And so the two begin to bond. articles.text: It all starts with faction writer Amor Towles The long days of summer beckon, and for many it’s time to begin preparing an aspirational list of potential good reads. Indeed… so many books and so little time; however, bear in mind that a good summer read should: 1) Never require a grudging effort (it’s not homework) 2) Ideally be a page-turner, meaning a narrative that you know you will miss when the last paragraph concludes 3) Immune to sand, sun, water 4) Balance nicely on your midsection when lying prone. I should begin by saying that I love to read. I always have, starting with comic books and the backs of cereal boxes. I soon graduated to anything resembling The Hardy Boys, and soon discovered a small local library just a short block from my house. It’s long been my habit to carry a book with me if I expected to be sitting in an airport, a waiting room, or anything akin to a coffee shop, park bench or a stretch of grass. Of course, I read for information (praise be Wikipedia), and treasure my MacBook Pro. But my bias has always been ink on paper fiction, hardcover or soft, with a richly imagined plot as well as compelling characters. I like the feel of holding a book, turning the pages. I keep a variety of bookmarks nearby, many embossed with the names of bookstores. I never turn down the corner of a page to mark where I stopped. To do so seems a kind of violation of, well, the integrity of the book. And, then there’s the experience of reading, pausing to consider a sentence or paragraph, reflecting on meaning, or letting your mind drift as connections to other aspects of life are made. I’ve always regarded that latter process a kind of meditation, an adjunct benefit to reading. As mentioned, I prefer fiction hence the four books I’m suggesting below are all by the America author Amor Towels. Some years ago a friend recommended that I read Towels’ debut novel, Rules of Civility, published in 2011. Knowing little about Towels, and unaware that his book was listed as a New York Times bestseller, I found a paperback edition and began my Towels reading experience. Rules proved to be a captivating good read. Set mainly in New York City, the novel opens on the last night of 1937 and continues into 1938. It is told from the point of view of 25-year-old Katey Kontent, who possesses a keen intellect and sharp wit. She journeys from a Wall Street secretarial pool into the upper echelon of New York society. Coming to Towels late, and having enjoyed Towels’ Rules for its plot and characters, I searched for his second novel, A Gentleman in Moscow. The story opens in 1922. Russian Count Alexander Rostov has been arrested, and on the orders of a Bolshevik tribunal is expected to be executed. Instead, he is given a life sentence of confinement in the lavish Moscow Metropol Hotel, and is quartered in a stark attic room, once used by the hotel’s servants. He is allowed to move about the hotel at will, to include the dining room where other visiting guests, part of the new post-Tsar elite, take their meals. A Gentleman in Moscow is in so many ways a compelling read, and Towels’ characters and plotting are extraordinary. And so I then waited for the much-anticipated release of his third book, titled The Lincoln Highway. It is set in 1954 and focuses on three young men with very different backgrounds. It is a road trip of sorts across America. For reasons I can’t quite explain, this narrative didn’t pull me in. But as I’m sure readers know, there must be an inexplicable connection between the reader and the story – timing is everything. I did finish the novel, and I may give it a second chance later. After a long hiatus, and reading a variety of other fiction, to include the novels of Michael Connelly which feature the durable L.A. detective Harry Bosch, I noticed that Amor Towels had published his fourth book, A Table for Two. There’s a tag line on the cover that says, “A Work of Fictions.” And to my surprise, the book is a collection of six short stories, set in New York in the year 2000, and a novella based in the golden days of Hollywood. I am more than halfway through the book, and have just begun the promised novella titled Eve in Hollywood, featuring Eve Ross, a character lifted from the pages of Rules of Civility. A word that has been used to describe Towels’ work is “sophistication.” I would add the word “stylish,” pointing to the author’s masterful descriptions and subtle plots that captivate, no matter the length of the narrative. At this moment I’m reading with anticipation about Eve in the Hollywood of 1938. And once again I am marveling at the rich prose and extraordinary imagination of this gifted writer.

articles.text: Kayakers are invited to join the UC Davis Tahoe Environmental Research Center (TERC) for the Fourth Annual Circumnavigate Lake Tahoe fundraiser supporting science around the lake and beyond. The event will take place over seven days, Monday through Sunday, June 17-23. Many people have paddled Lake Tahoe, but this event is unique. In addition to each day’s spectacular shoreline paddling, kayakers will see, share, and learn about Lake Tahoe’s ecology, geology and emerging challenges. TERC’s scientific experts will provide daily on-shore and on-water talks illustrating the science being used to restore and protect Lake Tahoe. Each day’s route is set near shore and extends 6-13 miles, with halfway rest stops on all but the shortest day. Experienced, professional kayak guides will lead the fleet. The odyssey starts at Sand Harbor, Nevada, and proceeds counterclockwise around the lake. (Daily details are provided after registration.) Paddlers will be shuttled by bus from takeout to put-in each day, to retrieve their cars. Multi-day paddlers will be also provided with onshore boat storage at each takeout. On the final day after paddling, there will be a gala party where paddlers can help to support TERC. The event is limited to 50 paddlers, and at the time of writing a few places remain. See https://tahoe.ucdavis.edu/events/ terc-circumnavigation-2024 for registration and more information. The backstory In the summer of 2020, longtime Piedmonter Scott Fitzgerrell, who now lives at Lake Tahoe, was building his fifth wooden sea kayak. Remarking to a friend, Dr. Geoff Schladow, then director of TERC, he said that once he “completed the doggone boat” he’d paddle it all the way around Lake Tahoe as a shakedown cruise. In that conversation was born the idea of inviting others to join the circumnavigation as a way of raising funds for TERC. Wildfire smoke put a halt to the event that summer, but in the clear skies of 2021, it was on with 35 paddlers eager to set forth. Now in its fourth year and UC Davis professor Dr. Alex Forrest delivers a talk at Whale Bay in Lake Tahoe. limited to only 50 paddlers, the event has become a must-do for kayakers as far away as Oregon Kayakers in the Tahoe Keys Scott Fitzgerrell in his new handmade wooden kayak and Illinois. Several have paddled all three years and are signed up for the fourth. It’s a unique event, especially given the on-beach and on-water lectures from UC Davis professors and TERC personnel. In addition to the learning opportunities, the route provides excellent wildlife viewing and wonderful views of every mile of the shoreline, including a stop in Emerald Bay. A graduate of Piedmont High School and UC Davis with Highest Honors, Emily also studied Drama at Oxford University. She enjoyed a much too brief but successful career in the Entertainment industry as an outstanding actor in film and television and as a film producer and playwright. At the time of her passing, Emily was an executive with Entertainment.net. Emily and husband Geordie are forever grateful to family members and friends who contributed to the GoFundMe effort. Emily will forever be remembered for her unending love, warmth, intelligence, creativity, energy, sense of humor and inclusiveness. A private family grave site service was held at East Lawn Cemetery in East Sacramento on May 19. articles.text: It had been a while since the group walked Crest Road just past Hampton Park. Crest is a long, slow climb and is a bit of a challenge, so members of Walking Wednesdays decided to go down rather than up. The group wend up Hampton Road, made their way to Estates Drive and then came down Somerset Road to Crest. The walkers continued to Hampton Road past Crocker Park to Hampton Park. The park was buzzing with students playing baseball and other games on a Wednesday morning. It was a group of fifth graders from Oakland’s Crocker Highlands School having their end-of-year field day. Drawing on Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s research, the park’s history was shared with the walkers. This land is part of 50 acres that Louis Titus, a Berkeley real estate developer purchased in 1911. Titus intended to build a mansion, but the new City of Piedmont raised property taxes dramatically in 1912, and he left town. In 1914, James Tyson, a lumber and shipping businessman, bought 30 acres of the land for his home. He was a strong supporter of Piedmont Boy Scouts, which began in 1910, and in 1921 Tyson made the land that is now Hampton Park available to the scouts for an outdoor camp. During the Great Depression in 1938, the Tysons also made the land available to the Piedmont schools. A WPA project leveled the land, which was intended to be the site of a future “East Piedmont” school. However, it was never built. In the 1950s and 60s, the space was a dusty, sometimes muddy little league baseball field. Later, youth soccer was played there often on a soggy field, as underground water was an ongoing problem. In 2000, the Piedmont Play School building was constructed at the back of the park. Dramatic improvements to the park were made during 2017 in a $2 million public/private partnership. articles.text: Mary Finley, a resident of Piedmont for more than 50 years, passed away peacefully on May 14, 2024 surrounded by her family. After the war, Mary’s family moved to the Elmwood district of Berkeley where she attended Berkeley High and UC Berkeley. She met her neighbor and future husband, Hugh Dozier Finley, on Christmas day in 1949. To be with Hugh on his deployment in Oahu, Hawaii, they agreed to forgo a traditional wedding and were married in a small ceremony on Whidbey Island in Washington in 1952. The park was buzzing with students playing baseball and other games on a Wednesday morning. It was a group of fifth graders from Oakland’s Crocker Highlands School having their end-of-year field day. Drawing on Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s research, the park’s history was shared with the walkers. This land is part of 50 acres that Louis Titus, a Berkeley real estate developer purchased in 1911. Titus intended to build a mansion, but the new City of Piedmont raised property taxes dramatically in 1912, and he left town. In 1914, James Tyson, a lumber and shipping businessman, bought 30 acres of the land for his home. A WPA project leveled the land, which was intended to be the site of a future “East Piedmont” school. However, it was never built. articles.text: Fourteen members of the Piedmont Seniors ventured to the South Bay where they learned about the two technology giants of the Bay Area, Google and Apple. Google recently opened its “Visitor Experience,” inside the company’s Gradient Canopy office building in Mountain View. This is the first Google brick and mortar retail outlet on the West Coast. The Seniors were a little tentative about exploring this “city within a city” as protestors had gathered there the day before. Fortunately, the campus was serene when the group arrived. The actual offices are not open to the public, but the Seniors still managed to explore the huge complex of buildings, open spaces and sculptured gardens. It was interesting to observe so many Google employees riding the company’s blue, yellow and A miniature bicycle offered by Google for its employees. Piedmont Seniors gather in front of Google’s Gradient Canopy office building. Members of the excursion included (front): Elizabeth Wierzbianska (left), Sue Getreuer, June Cohen, Lois Horwitz, Barbara Bigelow, Arlene Garfinkle (seated); (back) Mona Jamieson, Mary Buller, Carole Jones, Greg Jurin, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein and Edith Hereso. Not pictured: Jim Ayotte. Piedmont Seniors take a break at the Apple Visitors Center: Barbara Bigelow (left), Edith Hereso, Jane Cohen, Mona Jamieson, Lois Horwitz, Carole Jones, Janet Epstein and Mary Muller. The Apple Visitor Center in Cupertino red bicycles around the massive campus as they went from one office to another. The Google store even sells miniature versions of these iconic bicycles.The company retail store was built so that the public could experience some of the latest gadgets made by Google. The newest phones and other devices are tucked away in the store’s nooks and shelves, and there is a “high-tech” flavor to the store. The visitor center also includes the Huddle, where they offer free events and workshops for visitors. In fact, during this visit the Seniors witnessed a Google docent explaining some of the features of Google to the foreign press! After the tour, they had lunch at the newly opened Google Café. articles.text: The hotel quickly became a popular destination and drew visitors who passed a pleasant Sunday at Piedmont Springs, strolling the meandering paths to the mineral springs and enjoying an excellent lunch or dinner. The dining rooms served fresh meat from nearby ranches, milk and butter from Blair’s Dairy, and fresh fruit and vegetables from its gardens. The hotel also offered fine wine and liquor for those who did not care for mineral water. Fashionable San Franciscans would come for a week to escape the summer fog. Many hotel guests enjoyed the mild weather and views of San Francisco Bay and decided to buy land and build their homes here. The hotel thrived until 1892 when a spark from a faulty chimney started a fire on the roof. Hotel guests watched helplessly as the hotel burned to the ground before firefighters could arrive from downtown Oakland. The site would not be empty for long... but that’s another story. The mineral springs are still in Piedmont Park, but they were capped in the 1950s because the sulfur fumes offended many residents. The historical marker at the Veterans’ Building gives the location of the springs. To learn more about Piedmont’s history, see the Piedmont Historical Society website: Piedmonthistorical.org.
